deep_why: This work computes proofs that attest both to correct computation and the proper application of privacy noise in machine learning systems. The underlying principle is that cryptographic proofs create an unbreakable mathematical commitment: if a proof says a computation was done correctly, then it objectively was, because the proof would be computationally infeasible to forge. This principle applies here because the proving system encodes the exact rules of the privacy mechanism into mathematics—the prover cannot lie about whether noise was applied without invalidating the entire proof. By making privacy mechanisms verifiable without revealing their internals, this approach lets users trust that their data was handled carefully even when they cannot directly inspect the system.

This dataset addresses the task of condensing lengthy municipal meeting minutes into focused summaries of individual discussion subjects. The soundness rests on a fundamental principle: good summarization preserves the essential meaning of source text while cutting away details, and you can measure this fidelity by comparing summary wording against original passages. This principle holds for municipal documents because the core information—decisions made, positions stated, outcomes recorded—is stable regardless of how verbosely the original describes them. By providing manually written reference summaries paired with original documents, this benchmark lets researchers train and evaluate systems that learn to identify what truly matters in dense procedural text, solving the practical problem that citizens cannot feasibly read and extract meaning from thousands of lengthy meeting records.

The system computes a tamper-evident record of video footage by chaining cryptographic hashes into a blockchain ledger and storing copies across a decentralized network. This works because modifying even one frame of a video changes its hash, and that changed hash breaks the chain of subsequent hashes—tampering becomes immediately detectable. The principle holds here because the blockchain enforces chronological ordering that cannot be rewritten without redoing all subsequent blocks, a task that requires more computing power than an attacker typically possesses. By making any post-recording alteration leave an indelible mathematical trace, this approach lets security and legal systems identify whether footage is genuine or fake, solving the urgent problem of distinguishing real evidence from deepfakes.

This system reasons about what users will buy by examining sequences of their past actions (viewing, adding to cart, purchasing) as an expression of hidden logical rules they follow. The key principle is that confounding factors—unmeasured circumstances that influence behavior—can be separated from true causal effects by modeling the direct flow of influence from preference to behavior. This separation works because the system explicitly maps which preference at each step actually causes the next action, rather than just observing that earlier actions correlate with later ones. By isolating causal pathways from spurious patterns, the system generates explanations that genuinely reflect why users act, letting businesses understand and predict behavior more reliably than by simply pattern-matching past sequences.

This framework enhances language model performance on low-resource languages by injecting linguistic structure during training and then using a feedback loop during fine-tuning to identify and correct mistakes. The soundness rests on a principle from control theory: if you measure errors and feed that signal back to adjust what you train on next, you steer the learning process toward fixing those exact errors. This feedback works here because language errors are systematic—a model repeatedly makes the same type of mistake on similar inputs—so learning from past errors directly improves future performance. By combining bottom-up structural knowledge with top-down error correction, this approach lets systems work reliably on languages and dialects that lack large training datasets, expanding web-scale analysis to underrepresented communities.

The system speeds up long-context question answering by predicting which parts of retrieved documents the model will actually need to focus on, then fetching only those parts into fast memory. This works because models process information through attention mechanisms that concentrate on a few key phrases rather than reading everything equally—so the model that generates candidate answers can simultaneously identify which context it would attend to, creating a prediction without extra cost. This prediction is sound because the draft and main models share fundamental understanding of relevance even when they differ in sophistication. By eliminating the need to load and process irrelevant passages, this approach makes answering questions over thousands of documents practical, solving the latency bottleneck that previously limited real-world question systems.

This system adapts how an AI assistant interacts with users by continuously reading their facial expressions and gaze to infer whether they are engaged or overwhelmed, then adjusting reasoning depth and feedback timing accordingly. The principle is that cognitive state and decision quality are linked—people who are mentally exhausted make worse choices, and overloading them with information makes it worse—so matching the assistance level to their actual state optimizes both decision quality and mental comfort. This adaptation works here because the system responds in real-time to objective signals of cognitive strain rather than guessing from past behavior. By treating the user's moment-to-moment mental state as a control input that regulates how the system behaves, this approach makes decision support systems that genuinely help people think better, not just faster.

This study analyzes the ecosystem of commercial doxing services by collecting and categorizing messages and transaction links from underground channels, mapping how personal data flows from providers to resellers to buyers. The method is sound because systematic observation of marketplace structure and trading patterns reveals the mechanisms that make the business sustainable—what services are offered, how operators advertise, what payment methods enable transactions. This observation principle holds because underground markets, like legitimate ones, operate according to consistent patterns of supply and demand. By documenting these patterns empirically rather than speculatively, this work identifies specific points where interventions could disrupt illegal data trading, enabling regulators and platforms to target enforcement where it will have the greatest impact.

The attack exploits a mismatch in how guardrails and language models process text: guardrails break on small character changes (spaces, repetition, typos), but the underlying model remains robust and reconstructs intent from noisy input. This creates a security gap because the two systems were built independently and evolved along different paths—guardrails optimize for detecting obvious phrases while models learned to tolerate realistic text corruption. This gap is real because characters and semantics are fundamentally different layers: garbling characters only sometimes garbles meaning, especially for powerful models. By using both character noise and creative prompt rewording, adversaries can slip past the filter while remaining understandable to the model. This finding reveals that defense systems fail when components were not designed to fail together—security requires integration, not layering.

This system generates drug molecules by treating language model generation as a three-part process: encoding the protein target into a search space, exploring that space to find regions the model did not know about, and then carefully decoding candidates back into valid chemistry. This approach works because guided exploration breaks the false choice between staying within the model's training and generating nonsense—Bayesian optimization methodically searches for high-value molecules by testing predictions, while the surrogate model learns patterns from each test. This exploration principle applies because molecular design is a bounded optimization problem where structure matters more than memorization. By systematically probing unexplored but promising areas of design space, this method generates molecules that are both novel and chemically sound, letting researchers design drugs that exceed the training data rather than just recombining known examples.

This system coordinates multiple delivery drones using a physics-inspired model where each drone chooses actions based on an energy balance—travel cost plus service fairness plus avoiding other drones—with a temperature parameter that controls how much randomness enters decisions. The principle is that systems governed by such energy functions naturally minimize cost while spreading workload fairly, just as molecules in thermal equilibrium distribute according to probabilistic rules. This principle holds because the energy functions encode the actual problem constraints, and the Gibbs policy formally guarantees that high-energy (bad) outcomes become exponentially less likely as temperature drops. By treating fleet coordination as an analogy to statistical mechanics, this approach provides both a prediction tool (phase diagrams showing when coordination works well) and a control mechanism (tuning temperature to shift between efficiency regimes).

The system verifies scientific claims by breaking them into atomic facts, matching each fact to evidence snippets, checking support locally, and only searching the web when confidence is low. The soundness principle is calibration: if a fact-checker says it is uncertain about a claim, then web search should be used; if it is confident, local evidence is sufficient. This calibration works here because the checker is trained to be honest about what it knows—it learns to flag uncertain cases rather than guessing. This principle applies because scientific facts have consistent truth values, so a well-calibrated model can distinguish strong evidence from weak evidence. By coupling atomic-level fact checking with selective web corroboration only where needed, this approach reduces hallucination and prevents the system from overriding reliable context with contradictory web noise.

This work models price changes between centralized and decentralized exchanges as random walks following transition probabilities, then fits these probabilities to observed price data to discover when arbitrage opportunities emerge. The method works because Hidden Markov Models capture the idea that market regimes shift in predictable ways—high volatility days follow high volatility days, quiet periods persist—so once you identify which regime you are in, you can forecast the next likely price move. This principle applies to blockchain markets because prices genuinely do fluctuate with correlated shocks rather than moving randomly, and the blockchain ledger records every transaction, providing the exact data needed to fit the model. By learning these patterns from history, traders can time when price gaps are likely to close, turning a mathematical model of market behavior into a practical tool for profitable trading.

This system detects hateful memes by training a vision-language model to produce step-by-step reasoning chains that explain why an image is harmful, using rewards that favor both correct classification and coherent explanation. The principle is that reasoning that must be articulated step-by-step is harder to fake and more likely to identify genuine compositional meaning—when a model must explain how text interacts with imagery, it must reason about actual semantic relationships rather than memorizing surface patterns. This principle holds because hateful memes require understanding interaction between modalities, not just individual elements. By rewarding models for explanation quality alongside accuracy, this approach trains systems that genuinely understand why combinations are harmful, not just that they are, producing reliable detection that generalizes beyond the training set.

This short position argues that agentic artificial intelligence descends intellectually from the Semantic Web vision and Web Services architecture, and that applying formal methods from that era to modern AI agents would address unresolved foundational challenges. The principle underlying this historical argument is that apparently new problems often have prior solutions in abandoned frameworks, so understanding the lineage of ideas can reveal both what was tried before and why earlier attempts encountered obstacles. This principle applies here because agentic systems, like semantic web systems, require formal descriptions of what agents can do, how they coordinate, and how they maintain trust. By connecting contemporary agents to decades of formal work on service composition, this perspective offers the possibility that historical solutions—adapted to modern scale—could make agent systems more reliable and interpretable.
